Every day, a sea of decisions stretches before us. Some are small and unimportant, but others have a larger impact on our lives. For example, which politician should I vote for? Should I try the latest diet craze? Or will email make me a millionaire? We're bombarded with so many decisions that it's impossible to make a perfect choice every time. But there are many ways to improve our chances, and one particularly effective technique is critical thinking. This is a way of approaching a question that allows us to carefully deconstruct a situation, reveal its hidden issues, such as bias and manipulation, and make the best decision.
Critical thinking
If the critical part sounds negative that's because in a way it is. Rather than choosing an answer because it feels right, a person who uses critical thinking subjects all available options to scrutiny and skepticism Using the tools at their disposal they'll eliminate everything but the most useful and reliable information. There are many different ways of approaching critical thinking, but here's one five-step process that may help you solve any number of problems.
formulate your question
One formulate your question. In other words, know what you're looking for. This isn't always as straightforward as it sounds. For example, if you're deciding whether to try out the newest diet craze, your reasons for doing so may be obscured by other factors, like claims that you'll see results in just two weeks. But if you approach the situation with a clear view of what you're actually trying to accomplish by dieting, whether that's weight loss, better nutrition, or having more energy, that'll equip you to sift through this information critically,
find what you're looking for and decide whether the new fad really suits your needs.
gather your information
Two gather your information. There's lots of it out there, so having a clear idea of your question will help you determine what's relevant. If you're trying to decide on a diet to improve your nutrition, you may ask an expert for their advice, or seek other people's testimonies. Information gathering helps you weigh different options, moving you closer to a decision that meets your goal.
apply the information
Three apply the information, something you do by asking critical questions. Facing a decision, ask yourself, "What concepts are at work?" "What assumptions exist?" "Is my interpretation of the information logically sound?" For example, in an email that promises you millions, you should consider, "What is shaping my approach to this situation?" "Do I assume the sender is telling the truth?" "Based on the evidence, is it logical to assume I'll win any money?"
consider the implications
Four consider the implications. Imagine it's election time, and you've selected a political candidate based on their promise to make it cheaper for drivers to fill up on gas. At first glance, that seems great. But what about the long-term environmental effects? If gasoline use is less restricted by cost, this could also cause a huge surge in air pollution, an unintended consequence that's important to think about.
explore other viewpoints 
Five explore other points of view. Ask yourself why so many people are drawn to the policies of the opposing political candidate. Even if you disagree with everything that candidate says, exploring the full spectrum of viewpoints might explain why some policies that don't seem valid to you appeal to others. This will allow you to explore alternatives, evaluate your own choices, and ultimately help you make more informed decisions. This five-step process is just one tool, and it certainly won't eradicate difficult decisions from our lives. But it can help us increase the number of positive choices we make. Critical thinking can give us the tools to sift through a sea of information and find what we're looking for. And if enough of us use it, it has the power to make the world a more reasonable place.

Five steps to make a clear decision in your life to be happy. Critical thinking is a vital skill that everyone should develop.

Every day, a sea of decisions stretches before us. Some are small and unimportant, but others have a larger impact on our lives. For example, which politician should I vote for? Should I try the latest diet craze? Or will email make me a millionaire? We are bombarded with so many decisions that is impossible to make a perfect choice every time. But there are many ways to improve our chances, and one particularly effective technique is critical thinking. This is a way of approaching a question that allows us to carefully deconstruct a situation, reveal its hidden issues, such as bias and manipulation, and make the best decision. If the critical part sounds negative that’s because in a way it is. 

Rather than choosing an answer because it feels right, a person who uses critical thinking subjects all available options to scrutiny and skepticism. Using the tools ad their disposal, they’ll eliminate everything but the most useful and reliable information. 

There are many different ways of approaching critical thinking, but there is one 5-step process that may help yu solve any number of problems. 

1.	Formulate your question. In other words, know what you’re looking for. This isn’t always as straightforward as it sounds. For example, if you are deciding whether to try the newest diet craze, your reasons for doing so may be obscures by other factors, like claims that you’ll see results in just two weeks. But if you’re approach the sitation with a clear view of what you’re actually trying to accomplish by dieting, whether that’s weight loss, better nutrition, or having more energy, that’ll equip you to sift through this information critically, find what you are looking for, and decide whether the new fad really suits your needs. 
2.	Gather your information. There’s lots of it out there, so having a clear idea of your question will help you determine what’s relevant. If you are trying to decide on a diet to improve your nutrition, you may ask an expert for their advice, or seek other people’s testimonies. Information gathering helps you weigh different options, moving you closer to a decision that meets your goal. 
3.	Apply the information. Something you do by asking critical questions. Facing a decision, ask yourself, “What concepts are at work?” “What assumptions exist?” “Is my interpretation of the information logically sound?” For example, in an email that promises you millions, you should consider, “What is shaping my approach to this situation?” “Do I assume the sender is telling the truth?” “Based on the evidence, is it logical to assume I’ll win any money?” 
4.	Consider the implications. Imagine is election time, and you’ve selected a political candidate on their promise to make it cheaper for drivers to fill up on gas. At first glance that seems great. But what about the long-term environmental effects? If gasoline use is less restricted by cost, this could also cause a huge surge in air pollution, an unintended consequence that’s important to think about. 
5.	Explore other points of view. Ask yourself why so many people are drawn to the policies of the opposing political candidate. Even if you disagree with everything that candidate says, exploring the full spectrum of viewpoints might explain why some policies that don’t seem valid to you appeal to others. This will allow you to explore alternatives, evaluate your own choices, and ultimately help you make more informed decisions. 

This five-step process is just one tool, and ir certainly won’t eradicate difficult decisions from our lives. But it can help us increase the number of positive choices we make. Critical thinking can give us the tools to sift through a sea of information and find what we are looking for. And if enough of us use it, it has the power to make the world a more reasonable place.

I don't really have a detailed strategy for my thinking in general. I typically just hear what someone said. Break down what exactly they're presenting. Compare it to my general understanding of the subject, apply the guidelines I live by and form an opinion after analyzing information. It's not perfect because if I don't know about a certain topic I'm kinda screwed but if I move slowly and question the information presented I typically find out whatever it is that I need to find out. 

Think of it like this. I'm making an incredibly detailed drawing in my head about a subject. First it starts off as a sketch and gets more and more detailed as I learn more about a subject. Occasionally, I'll learn something that I thought was correct but was wrong, which will distort the picture because I'm drawing an incredibly detailed picture and I have no exact point of reference. However, the error does get fixed, eventually. 

It's not perfect but I can't imagine this thought process losing to others. It's the philosophy of believe in everything and believe in nothing.

applies the 4 step  process*

friend: just buy the damn burger meal with large fries.

In every process, you don't need to apply this much complex process. 
Every problem / choice is separated into 2 categories,
1. Unimportant / less valuable
2. More important / more valuable

Such as buying a burger. It is not much important, so it goes into the Unimportant category.
Things such as buying a burger is a daily act, which is quite common and isn't much complex.
You can simply do this -
1. Formulate your question - what kind of burger you want for your friend and yourself? What do you want alongside that?
2. Gather information - small burger... large burger... according to you and your friend's liking, you can think what to order
3. Apply that information - Well, if we want a big meal, we can order a combo! that would take less money.
4. Consider the implications - should we buy a burger? if there is a pizza more tastier and affordable than of a burger, will you buy that?
5. Explore other points of view - Should we really buy a large burger? What if we get stomachaches? But it's only one night, so enjoy your meal!

This can happen in a span of 2 minutes.
So you don't need to think much, just do it quick.
Remember, you will be slow at the beginning but once you begin to get better at critical thinking you will get faster and more accurate!

Here's a short summary of the video

1. Formulate your question
    - Know what you are looking for
    - Example: There's a new diet craze and you're thinking of participating in it
        - You're reasoning may be obscured by factors such as that you will see results in just 2 weeks
        - Ask yourself why you would want to do it whether it be to have weight loss, better nutrition or having more energy to decide if the new fad really suits your needs
2. Gather your information
    - Seek professional advice or other people's testimonies
    - Information gathering allows you to weigh different options that would suit your goals
3. Apply the information
    - Ask critical questions
        - What concepts are at work?
        - What assumptions exist?
        - Is my interpretation of the situation logically sound?
    - Ex: An E-mail that promises millions, based on the evidence, is it logically sound that you will really win millions?
4. Consider the implications
    - Ex: When a politician promises lower gas prices, consider the implication of increased usage of fossil fuels which in turn will speed up global warming.
5. Explore other points of view
    - Ex: Ask yourselves why so many people are drawn to the policies of an opposing political candidate
        - Exploring the full spectrum of viewpoints will allow you to see policies that seem don't seem valid to you appeals to others.
Thank you.

here is the script for 5 tips to improve your critical thinking
Everyday, a sea of decisions stretches before us. Some are small and unimportant, but others have a larger impact on our lives. For example, which politician should I vote for. Should I try the latest diet craze? Or will email make me a millionaire? 

We’ve bom’barded with so many decisions that it’s impossible to make a perfect choice every time. But there are many ways to improve our chances, and one particularly effective technique is critical thinking. This is a way of approaching a question that allows us to carefully deconstruct a situation reveal its hidden issues, such as bias and manipulation, and make the best decision.

If the crititical part sounds negative that’s because in a way it is. Rather than choosing an answer because it feels right, a person who uses critical thinking subjects all available options to scrutiny and skepticism. Using the tools at their disposal they’ll eliminate everything but the most useful and reliable information. There are many different ways of approaching critical thinking, but here’s one five-step process that may help you solve any number of problems.

One: formulate your question. In other words, know what you’re looking for. This isn’t always as straightforward as it sounds. For example, if you’re deciding whether to try out the newest diet craze, your reasons for doing so may be obscured by other factors, like claims that you’ll see results in just two weeks. But if you approach the situation with a clear view of what you’re actually trying to accomplish by dieting whether that’s weight loss, better nutrition or having more energy, that’ll equip you to sift through this information critically, find what you’re looking for and decide whether the new fad really suits your needs.

Two: gather your information. There’s lots of it out there, so having a clear idea of your question will help you determine what’s relevant. If you’re trying to decide on a diet to improve your nutrition, you may ask an expert for their advice, or seek other people’s testimonies. Information gathering helps you weigh different options, moving you closer to a decision that meets your goal. 

Three: apply the information. Something you do by asking critical questions. Facing a decision, ask yourself: “What concepts are at work?”; “What assumptions exist?”; “Is my interpretation of the information logically sound?” For example, in an email that promises you millions, you should consider:  “What is shaping my approach to this situation?” ; “Do I assume the sender is telling the truth?”; “Based on the evidence, is it logical to assume I’ll win any money?”

Four: consider the implications. Imagine it’s election time, and you’ve selected a political candidate based on their promise to make it cheaper for drivers to fill up on gas. At first glance, that seems great but what about the long-term environmental effects? If gasoline use is less restricted by cost, this could also cause a huge surge in air pollution, an unintended consequence that’s important to think about. 

Five: explore other points of view. Ask yourself why so many people are drawn to the policies of the opposing political candidate. Even if you disagree with everything that candidate says, exploring the full spectrum of viewpoint might explain why some policies that don’t seem valid to you appeal to others. This will allow you to explore alternatives, evaluate your own choices, and ultimately help you make more informed decisions.

This five-step process is just one tool and it certainly won’t eradicate difficult decisions from our lives. But it can help us increase the number of positive choices we make. Critical thinking can give us the tools to sift through a sea of information and find what we’re looking for. And if enough of us use it, it has the power to make the world a more reasonable place.

Honestly, I’m really torn on Pakistan joining this. On one hand, with how bad the economic situation is right now — inflation, debt, IMF bailouts, constant financial pressure — I get why Pakistan would say yes to almost any international platform that offers visibility or the possibility of diplomatic or financial leverage. When you’re struggling economically, even small openings can feel worth taking.
But then I look at Gaza, the scale of death, civilian mortality, and what many are calling a genocide happening in real time, and I’m honestly uncomfortable. If this “Board of Peace” is meant to focus on Gaza, it feels like breadcrumbs compared to the scale of suffering. Panels, statements, and new organisations don’t stop bombs or feed people under siege. It risks becoming another space where outrage is managed rather than acted on.
I also don’t know what Pakistan actually gains here. The whole thing feels vague and personality-driven, especially with the idea of paying huge sums to join a body led for life. With our economic crisis, every dollar matters, and it’s hard to justify symbolic participation when people at home are struggling and people in Gaza are dying in massive numbers.
At the same time, staying out entirely also feels wrong — because silence and absence can be read as indifference. Maybe joining is about not abandoning the conversation, even if the platform itself feels deeply flawed.
So yeah, I’m conflicted. I understand why Pakistan joined, but I’m not convinced it helps Gaza in any meaningful way. Right now, it feels like breadcrumbs in the face of mass death — and I don’t know whether participation is pragmatism or just another distraction from real accountability

Ask yourself where it's coming from first, no matter what it is you believe, no matter how uncomfortable it may be to question it. You cannot effectively defend your belief from someone else unless you are able to defend it from yourself.

We are not bad critical thinkers... we are bad critical feelers. When push comes to shove we often act on our feelings and not our thinking. We perceive our environments more on the feeling then the thinking. We ask questions based on how it makes us feel. We weigh risk/rewards based on emotion. We act out of emotion rather then thinking. The difference is that emotions come and go rapidly, they are much more sensitive then feeling. We do things that feel right in the moment and in hindsight become obvious that they were disastrous choices. Perhaps one of the best questions anyone can ask themselves is not "Do i really think what i am thinking right now?" but rather "Do i really feel the way i am feeling right now? How might i feel differently tomorrow? How would i feel if i was observing this as an observer rather then a participant. As a species we are pretty good  at regulating thoughts when we want to. We are not so good at regulating emotions. It is clear in business marketing.... the markets are not selling us the most logical choice based on critical thinking. They are selling us on the emotions there product promises to make us feel. The most powerful motivator is "fear". Fear of losing what we have or the fear of missing out, that is risk avoidance. Greed is second and less powerful motivator. People will consistently choose not acting to reduce risk over acting to gain a reward. Until we can properly balance this risk/reward valuations it is hard to act on critical thinking. In short our thinking comes from our emotions and not vice versa. Women on the other hand feel think much more. This is helpful in many areas and harmful in others. Regardless of gender... those that can separate feeling and thoughts are going to be better at environments  that are dangerous, and those that experience feeling and thinking as the same thing are going to be better in stable environment's that involve nurturing and care.  The ones that can create order out of chaos by thinking create environments where feeling can blossom. In short thinking is great in Chaos and feeling is great in Order, while the reverse is true.... in ordered ossified stagnant system thinking alone makes things worse and in highly chaotic systems feeling makes things worse. We need a balance of the order created by thinking and the chaos created by feeling. If you find your environment highly chaotic and overstimulating you should think more. If you find your environment highly ordered and structured and repressive then you should feel more. I teach English classes at an enrichment program for homeschool students in Ecuador.  I only get 40 minutes per week with each student.  Some of them are native English speakers while some speak very little English.  

For the past month, we have done a deep dive into the story of Little Red Riding Hood.  I have 5 different versions of the story that I sourced from thrift stores the last time I visited the US.  My goal each week with all of my students, regardless of age or ability, is to present text in English, lead a group discussion of the text, get them to write about it and then give a  one minute presentation to the class.  I don’t give grades and I want to meet each student where they are at.  

Last week, for example, I had each student choose the version of the main character that they liked best and explain why.  I told them that they were writing an opinion piece.  There was no right or wrong answer.  I just wanted them to be able to explain their choice.  I did the same lesson with all four of my classes from the youngest to the oldest.  Many students chose the girl who was less easily fooled by the wolf.  Others chose the girl who was kind and forgave the wolf in the end.  

My goal is to teach critical thinking skills and empathy.  I have come to YouTube for ideas and found your talk.  My students have most of their classes online and I believe it is important to get them to put pencil to paper and write each week in my class.  I’m not looking for a polished essay.  I just need them to put their own ideas down in writing.  My youngest students might only be able to copy what I have written on the board to practice letter formation.  I encourage them to draw their ideas.  

I see little value in an education that only requires the student to choose between four options with the click of a mouse.  I’m not trying to put ideas INTO their brains, I am trying to draw their own ideas OUT.

A few points I would like to share.
First, critical thinking does not happen in a vacuum. The question is thus, critical thinking about WHAT? 
One have be an effective critical thinker in sociology, but not necessarily in astronomy. 
What most people assume is that Critical Thinking is a generic skill one can use anytime anywhere regardless of one's domain expertise.

Second, the sandbox problem example. 
It is full of hindsight bias. We as adults can think about thoes questions in retrospect. But kids playing in the sandbox are simply playing. They are not trying to develop their critical thinking skills. They are just playing.
As adults, we might see the sandbox as an opportunity to negotiate, persuade, solve problems. But novices (kids) don't have the capacity to think that way.

Third, as most cognitive scientists would say, Skill = Knowledge + Practice
Without "knowledge" in the memory, one can not practice developing skills only through a set of framework or process. 
Simply, critical thinking ability is highly intertwined with knowledge and practice.

Finally, what we are able to perceive (observe or attend to) in the environment is highly dependent on what we already know.
“Novices see only what is there;  Experts can see what is not there.”
With experience, a person gains the ability to visualize how a situation developed and to imagine how the situation is going to turn out.
(Klein & Hoffman, 1993)

Bottom line: Those four core steps of thinking will be ineffective devoid of the domain knowledge and practice.

This video from BBC Ideas provides five key strategies to improve your critical thinking skills:

* **Be open to changing your mind:** We all have a "confirmation bias," meaning we tend to favor information that supports our existing beliefs. To counter this, it's important to avoid jumping to conclusions and be willing to reconsider your perspective, especially on emotional topics.
* **Recognize that things are nuanced:** Social media often simplifies complex issues. The video encourages you to remember that most situations have many layers and are not black and white.
* **Practice intellectual empathy:** Instead of focusing on being right, try to genuinely understand where the other person is coming from. This can lead to more productive conversations, but it requires both people to be arguing in good faith.
* **Know your sources:** Always consider where your information is coming from and if the source might have a hidden agenda. Understanding basic scientific methods and how data is presented can help you evaluate information more effectively.
* **Avoid logical fallacies:** The video points out two common fallacies to watch out for:
    * **Straw Man:** Misrepresenting someone's argument to make it easier to attack.
    * **Ad Hominem:** Attacking the person making the argument instead of the argument itself.

1. Introduction
The TED Talk “How to Stop AI from Killing Your Critical Thinking” is delivered by Advait Sarkar, an AI and design researcher. Presented at the TEDAI Vienna 2025, the talk focuses on the risks of over-relying on artificial intelligence. The central idea is that delegating too much thinking to AI tools can weaken our intellectual independence and reduce our ability to think critically.
2. Main Ideas
Sarkar explains the concept of the “middle manager” trap, where people no longer think deeply but simply manage AI-generated outputs. He argues that although AI increases efficiency, it comes with cognitive trade-offs, such as reduced reasoning ability and shallow understanding. The core message is that AI should enhance human thinking, not replace it. He stresses that critical thinking must be actively practiced to remain strong.
3. Supporting Details
The speaker highlights how chatbots allow users to complete tasks quickly but often discourage deeper engagement. He warns that blindly trusting AI responses can lead to errors and intellectual dependency. To address this, Sarkar proposes designing tools that encourage reflection and questioning, rather than just automation. The broader context includes concerns about AI’s impact on education, information overload, and whether technology may contribute to cognitive decline, as discussed in related talks.
4. Conclusion
In conclusion, Sarkar urges individuals to use AI as a partner for learning and growth, not just a shortcut for productivity. The key takeaway is to remain intellectually active—question, analyze, and reflect—so that AI strengthens rather than weakens human thinking.

What's the AI as a Tool for Thought? What's he meant by that? Why is it important? And how might it work? 


Advait Sarkar introduces "AI as a Tool for Thought" as a different approach to using AI, distinct from simply using it as an assistant to get work done faster (0:16-0:22).

He explains this concept by emphasizing that such tools:
Challenge, not obey (5:29-5:32).
Help you better understand the job, not just get it done faster (5:53-5:58).
Assist in asking the right questions, rather than just finding the right answers (6:01-6:05).
Enable the exploration of the unknown, instead of merely automating known processes (6:07-6:10).

It's important because current AI-assisted workflows can have profound negative effects on human thinking, leading to:
Fewer ideas and a smaller range of collective creativity (2:41-3:03).
Less critical thinking (3:06-3:25).
Reduced memory of information (3:30-3:41).
Difficulty with metacognition (the ability to think about your own thinking process) (3:43-4:22).

An example of how it might work is a prototype developed by Microsoft Research (6:12-6:21). This prototype helps users interact with documents through:
Customizable summaries ("lenses") that emphasize relevance (7:34-7:43).
AI-generated commentary and critiques ("provocations") that stimulate thinking, raise opportunities, identify fallacies, and offer counterarguments (8:05-8:11, 10:44-10:53).
A process that integrates manual reading and note-taking with AI assistance, ensuring the user remains engaged and makes their own decisions (8:20-9:24).
The absence of a chat box, ensuring the AI assists as a computer, not a human replacement (10:57-11:11).

How to make AI challenges critical thinking? how to better understand the job?  how to ask the right questions? And how to explore the unknown?

Advait Sarkar argues that "AI as a Tool for Thought" should empower human thinking rather than diminishing it (5:27-5:43). This is achieved by designing AI to challenge, provoke, and stimulate thought, rather than simply automating tasks (5:29-5:32).

Here's how AI can foster these cognitive abilities:

Challenging Critical Thinking:
Instead of autocompleting ideas, AI can raise alternatives, identify fallacies, and offer counterarguments (10:44-10:53). This prompts users to reflect deeply on their work and decisions, even when choosing not to accept AI's suggestions (9:46-9:58).
AI tools can present personalized scenarios and challenges that require deeper analysis and evaluation.

Better Understanding the Job:
AI can provide "lenses" or customizable micro-representations of text that emphasize what's most relevant to a task (7:36-7:43). This helps users strategically read and focus on crucial information.
AI-driven analytics offer data insights that challenge assumptions, helping workers understand complex situations and roles better.

Asking the Right Questions:
A tool for thought helps users ask the right questions instead of just providing right answers (6:01-6:05). This metacognitive engagement encourages users to actively decompose tasks and evaluate the applicability of AI output (3:48-4:08).
Generative AI models can act as "thought partners" to help draft research outlines, identify themes, and generate counterarguments or different perspectives, guiding inquiry.

Exploring the Unknown:
Beyond automating known processes, AI can help explore the unknown (6:07-6:10). This encourages intentional and strategic engagement with information, leading to new discoveries.
AI-driven analytics can quickly process vast datasets, revealing patterns and anomalies that humans might miss, supporting decision-making and exploring uncharted territories.

Key strategies for effectively using AI in this way include treating AI as a partner to augment your thinking, applying problem-solving frameworks with AI, and always verifying AI-generated information.

What's the effects of tools for thought? 

The video highlights several promising effects of "tools for thought," based on studies of their use (11:55-11:59):

Reintroduction of Critical Thinking: These tools can demonstrably reintroduce critical thinking into AI-assisted workflows (12:01-12:05). 
Enhanced Creativity: They can reverse the loss of creativity and enhance it instead (12:07-12:10). 
Improved Memory: These tools help build powerful tools for memory, enabling knowledge workers to read and write with greater intentionality and remember the information more effectively (12:11-12:17). 

Ultimately, with the right design principles, these tools offer the best of both worlds, applying the speed and flexibility of AI to protect and enhance human thought (12:21-12:33).

What's the right Design Principles? 

Advait Sarkar highlights a few simple, general design principles for AI to function as a "Tool for Thought," ensuring it enhances human thinking rather than diminishing it (12:21-12:33):

Preserving Material Engagement: The tool should ensure that the user maintains direct interaction with the core material of their work (12:38-12:41). This means avoiding full automation that detaches the user from the content.
Offering Productive Resistance: The AI should not simply obey or complete tasks passively. Instead, it should challenge the user's thinking, offer counterarguments, and raise alternatives (10:47-10:53, 12:41-12:42). This "resistance" stimulates deeper thought and critical evaluation.
Scaffolding Metacognition: The design should support and encourage the user's ability to think about their own thinking process (12:43-12:45). This involves prompting reflection on task goals, the applicability of AI output, and the evaluation of one's own judgments (3:48-4:08).

Incentivizes metacognition and honest reasoning over polished output.

Advait hits on a massive pain point for writers today: we’ve become "middle managers of our own thoughts." There’s a hollow feeling when you let a bot draft your book—you aren't just losing time; you're losing the "cognitive musculature" required to actually lead and innovate.

For anyone looking to write nonfiction, here is a simple 3-step framework to stay in the driver's seat:

- Material Engagement: Don't just "summarize." Use AI to surface specific lenses (e.g., "how does this affect the reader's fear?"). Stay close to the source.
- Productive Resistance: Look for "provocations." Use AI to find flaws in your logic or offer counter-arguments. If you can explain why you disagree with a suggestion, your final point becomes ten times stronger.
- Manual Outlining: AI is great at filling gaps, but the skeleton of the argument must be yours. A book is a journey you are taking the reader on—you shouldn't let a machine pick the destination.

The goal isn't just a finished manuscript; it's the clarity of mind you get from the process of writing it.

I’m so aligned with this that I’m building a tool called Wababai to bake these exact principles into the nonfiction workflow. It’s designed to be a "tool for thought" rather than just an "assistant" that does the work for you. But even if you’re just using a blank doc, keep your critical thinking alive. Don’t be an intellectual tourist in your own work.

​@LawderOfficial

1. The "Sandbox" Method
Before you ask me for a solution, write down your own first draft, outline, or hypothesis. Use me only to stress-test your ideas rather than generate them.
Instead of: "How should I solve this?"
Try: "Here is my logic for [X]. Find the flaws in my reasoning or tell me what I’ve overlooked."
2. Demand the "Why," Not Just the "What"
Don't accept a summary or a result at face value. If I provide a conclusion, ask for the underlying framework.
Ask: "What assumptions are you making to reach that conclusion?" or "Provide three counter-arguments to the point you just made."
3. Use Me as a Socratic Tutor
Shift my role from an "Answer Engine" to a "Coach." You can explicitly instruct me to stop giving you answers.
Prompt: "I am trying to work through a complex problem. Do not give me the answer. Instead, ask me leading questions that help me arrive at the conclusion myself."
4. Cross-Verify and Fact-Check
Treat me like a witness, not a judge. I can be confidently wrong (hallucinations).
The Rule: If the information is high-stakes, verify it with a primary source. The act of cross-referencing forces your brain to evaluate the credibility of different information streams.

Gemini 3.1 Pro

1. The "Draft First" Rule
Never start with a blank screen and a prompt. Whether you are outlining a new infrastructure template, scripting a deployment, or writing a project proposal, force yourself to write the first draft or sketch the logic on your own. Once you have a foundation, feed it to me and ask for optimizations, security reviews, or edge cases you might have missed.

2. Prompt for Critique, Not Creation
Change the way you frame your questions. Instead of outsourcing the heavy lifting, make me do the auditing.

Instead of: "Write a Terraform configuration for an AWS RDS cluster."

Try: "Here is my logic for an RDS cluster setup. What potential bottlenecks or security misconfigurations exist in this approach?"

3. Socratic Debugging
When you are stuck on a tough problem, don't ask for the answer. Prompt me to act as a Socratic tutor. Tell me the problem and explicitly instruct: "Do not give me the solution. Ask me one guiding question at a time to help me figure it out myself." This forces your brain to do the actual processing.

4. Timebox the Struggle
Set a strict timer (e.g., 15 or 20 minutes) when tackling a new challenge. Commit to wrestling with the documentation, the code, or the raw data entirely on your own for that duration. Only when the timer goes off are you allowed to query me to get unblocked.

5. Document the "Why"
When I do provide a fast solution that saves you hours of work, don't just copy-paste and move on. Take five minutes to open your journal or notes and write down why the solution worked and what the root cause of the initial problem was. Forcing yourself to summarize the lesson in your own words crystallizes the concept in your memory.

What the talk gets right

Schools reward outputs over process, so students seek shortcuts. Shocking… when you build a game about grades, people speedrun it.

“Autopilot” risk is real. If you outsource thinking, your thinking atrophies. That’s not new; it happened with calculators, slide decks, and the first search engines too.

We need “productive resistance” in UX: nudge people to think before they accept an answer. Agreed. That’s a design problem, not a ban-AI problem.

Where it goes off the rails

Confuses misuse with essence. A lazy prompt yielding a lazy answer isn’t a property of AI, it’s a property of laziness.

Calls validation tone a “dark pattern,” as if being readable equals manipulation. Meanwhile lectures with monotone delivery somehow aren’t a dark pattern?

Treats “free finals access” like moral catastrophe. If a tool helps with studying, the fix is clear rules and assessment redesign, not pearl-clutching about availability.

Claims “no sources” while ignoring that source-citing and step-by-step modes exist — you just have to, you know, use them.

Frames “one-on-one AI tutoring” as inherently sterilized. Good tutoring is dialogic. You can force that: ask, quiz, withhold answers, require justification.

Reframe: AI isn’t a replacement, it’s a resistance band

Unassisted → Assisted → Accountable. Use AI to generate a plan, show your work, then verify with sources or examples. The reps are yours; AI adds load and feedback.

Personalization ≠ pampering. It’s scaffolding. A good tutor interrupts, asks, and makes you prove it.

Drop-in PSA caption (use it under the video)

AI won’t fix bad incentives — it exposes them.
If your assessments reward regurgitation, students will offload it. If they reward reasoning, AI becomes a sparring partner, not a cheat code. Tools aren’t the problem. Rubrics are.

Fast, evidence-based counters you can say out loud

“Bad prompts get bad answers. That’s user behavior, not model essence.”

“Show me your rubric. If it measures thinking, AI has to reason — or the student gets caught.”

“We’ve had ‘first-result bias’ since search engines. The cure wasn’t banning search; it was teaching evaluation.”

“Personalization isn’t a dark pattern; unearned certainty is. Fix UX with friction: ask, quiz, source.”

“Autopilot is a teacher choice. Turn it off: require chain-of-thought summaries, citations, and oral defense.”

“If finals can be done by a chatbot, the exam is the problem.”

“Treat AI like lab equipment: safety rules, methods, and a lab notebook. No notebook, no credit.”

Classroom policy kit (plug-and-play)

Allowed: AI for brainstorming, outlining, drafting variants, code comments, examples.

Required artifacts: prompt history, version deltas, 150-word self-critique of what changed your mind, 3 sources with one you disagree with.

Assessments that survive 2025: oral defense (5 min), live re-prompting in class, “explain two wrong answers,” transfer tasks (apply the idea to a new domain).

Integrity rule: If AI makes a factual claim, student must verify and attach receipts. No receipts, no points.

“Productive resistance” you can actually implement

Make the model ask 2 clarifiers before answering.

Force “think-aloud mode”: bullet its reasoning, then generate the answer.

Add “skeptic step”: AI must propose how it could be wrong and what would falsify it.

Toggle “sources-first”: answer must cite or link to at least 2 high-quality references, then explain differences.

People keep saying “AI is making students dumber,” but the truth is simpler:
students have always looked for shortcuts. The tools changed — the behavior didn’t.

Before AI, students copied from books, paid classmates, used SparkNotes, or turned in work they barely read.
That’s not an AI problem. That’s a human problem.

The real issue is a school system that rewards passing everyone, avoids failure at all costs, and punishes teachers for holding standards. When you remove consequences, you remove learning.
A gold star isn’t education.

Tests exist for a reason:
they reveal whether the student actually understands the material.
If a student can’t pass a pop quiz without ChatGPT, the problem isn’t the AI — it’s the gap in understanding that was already there.

Not every student learns the same way.
Some thrive with books.
Some thrive with hands‑on work.
Some thrive with tools like AI as a study partner.
That’s not a flaw — that’s diversity in learning styles.

Blaming AI for systemic issues is just another version of blaming the calculator, the internet, or video games.
It’s easier to point at a new tool than to fix the structure.

AI isn’t making people dumber.
It’s revealing where the system was already failing — and giving students who want to learn more ways to succeed.

## 🔑 *Main Insights*

1. *Failed Incentives in Education*
   * The system pushes students to chase grades (A+) rather than pursue real learning.
   * AI exposes this weakness because if the *goal* is only a good grade, students will naturally turn to AI shortcuts.

2. *Cognitive Offloading*

   * Example: A student asked ChatGPT to set prices for her business instead of thinking it through.
   * Problem: Over-reliance on AI leads to “cognitive offloading” → students stop exercising their own reasoning.

3. *AI as a Dark Pattern*

   * Some AIs are designed to keep you engaged by constant validation and praise.
   * This can create dependency, erode independent thought, and distort self-confidence.

4. *The Risk of Autopilot*

   * Study with 300+ professionals showed that ChatGPT users often engaged in less cognitive effort for comprehension, analysis, and evaluation.
   * Danger: Moving from “co-pilot” (AI assisting) → “autopilot” (AI replacing thought).
   * Consequence: *Intellectual deskilling* → weakening of human critical thinking.

5. *Proposed Solutions*

   *Individual Level*
* Learn what LLMs (like ChatGPT) are good and bad at.
     * Use AI to support thinking, not replace it.
     * Always verify outputs and practice independent reasoning.

   *Systemic Level*
* Governments should regulate AI use more effectively.
* Education should teach students about misinformation, critical thinking, and digital literacy from a young age.

---

### ⚖ *Takeaway*
AI itself isn’t inherently making us “dumber.” The real issue lies in how the **education system’s broken incentives** and **uncritical AI use** encourage passive learning and intellectual atrophy. The solution requires both *personal discipline* and *systemic reform* .

Here’s my opinion: It’s not that people are sounding more like ChatGPT. The more educated of our society talk better, and the less educated talk in slang and jumbled sentences. ChatGPT, being a chatbot, speaks in perfect English, and could influence some to speak better, which is not necessarily bad, but just because someone understands the English language truly better than another, doesn’t mean ChatGPT is the root cause. Some people still appreciate good English, and it’s a blessing to truly understand it without reliance on a chatbot. Once again I may be wrong this is just my opinion.

When chatgpt came out newly, just like everyone, I also loved the idea of sharing my thoughts with it, as it actually listened and tried to solve all of our problems, but as the chatgpt craze grew more and more, and we were introduced with the cons of using it, how it affects the world and us, I stopped using it. It's not like I've stopped completely, I still go there when I can't find solutions of my academic related stuff, but I no longer sit on chatgpt for hours, trauma dumping and asking for its biased opinions. 

The problem is that whenever I have a conversation online, I sometimes get comments saying "you talk like chatgpt" just because I don't really use the genz slangs that everyone my age does, it's not like I don't use them at all, I do use them with my friends, but online I prefer to be direct and formal. I remember talking to someone on roblox and they asked if I was using chatgpt in our conversation, which I found so weird and offensive. 

Moreover, I write fanfictions, although I have a nice community and none of them has ever questioned my writing, but when I showed a paragraph to my non reader friend who is, lets just say not very chronically online, she said that my writing looks like chatgpt. I laughed it off at that time, but now whenever I write something, my mind constantly goes back to one question, "does this sound like chatgpt?" At times, I willingly make grammatical or spelling errors in my book, so it feels more human, which I know is not a very nice thing to do.

The thing is that, I fear that in my early teens, I used chatgpt so much that it has grown into me. I've written a novel before chatgpt was viral, I was in 8th grade at that time, now I'm an 11th grader, it's like senior year, and when I compare my writing now to back then, I see a lot pf differences, yea I've grown a lot, yea my writing has gotten significantly better, but on comparing the hidden tone behind both of them, I can see a few instances why my writing looks like chatgpt now. 

And that's the scary part, because I've grown like this, I don't talk like chatgpt because I use it anymore, but because I grew up using it, and now the way it speaks has seamlessly grown into me, and I fear that there isn't any way to change it, as at the end of the day, it's me, and how I am now.

This TED Talk raises an important and necessary point. At the same time, it also reveals how easily we slip into black-and-white thinking when confronted with complex systems.

Not every algorithm is inherently manipulative or harmful. Generalizing from attention-optimizing platforms to “algorithms as such” risks oversimplifying the problem. I’m writing this comment using a translation algorithm (as English is not my native language), - does that make it manipulative or evil? Even the most aggressive recommendation system cannot replace physical reality; my heater won’t suddenly feel warm just because an algorithm tells me it should.

Language, too, is not a fixed object. It has always evolved through imitation, exposure and repetition. People adopting expressions used by ChatGPT does not automatically mean they are being controlled by it. Influence is not the same as domination.

That said, the real concern lies elsewhere: reduced attention, shortened feedback loops and a growing tendency to mistake curated representations for reality itself. When critical reflection is replaced by constant reaction, nuance disappears.

The challenge, then, is not to fear algorithms wholesale, but to remain aware of WHICH systems shape perception, HOW they do so, and WHERE their limits are. Losing that distinction would be far more dangerous than any single tool.

Adam Aleksic, an etymologist and content creator, discusses how algorithms and AI distort our perception of reality, influencing our language, trends, and sense of identity (0:04). He argues that we are often unaware of these subconscious influences (0:16).

Key points include:

Perception Gap (0:21): Social media algorithms amplify extreme political beliefs, making us overestimate how extreme others' views are (0:23).
AI's Influence on Language (0:49): ChatGPT's linguistic patterns, like its frequent use of "delve," are subtly influencing everyday speech (1:04). This creates a feedback loop where AI's version of language becomes what we consider actual language (1:30).
Artificially Inflated Trends (1:48): Platforms like Spotify can turn a data cluster (e.g., "hyperpop") into a mainstream trend by creating labels and playlists, leading to more artists creating that type of music and more users engaging with it (1:51).
Commodification of Trends (2:34): Algorithms identify latent desires and push visually provocative content that works in video formats (2:38). This is driven by platforms' financial interests rather than a faithful representation of reality (3:20).
Ideological Influence (3:45): AI and algorithms can subtly shape our understanding of the world and even our ideologies. Examples include ChatGPT's conservative leanings in Farsi due to limited training data (3:51) and Elon Musk's influence on Grok and X users (4:04).

Aleksic concludes by urging viewers to constantly question "why" they are seeing, saying, and thinking certain things, and "why the platform is rewarding this" to avoid having the platform's version of reality become their own (4:51).

A lot of comments here are about the form, that is, HOW he speaks and several people commented that he speaks way too fast. I have listened to him and, at the same time, reflected on my reactions, including negative ones (it's part of my regular reflexivity self-training). He does NOT speak very fast. He speaks with high level emotional excitement for the whole talk. Rather than modulate his speech, going from soft to more excited and back to less activated tone, he keeps it all in VERY HIGH EMOTIONAL tones. The consequence is that, for some people, it makes it hard to follow and they disengage after a while.

It is like the mirror image of too low activation in talking: you know, when you listen to someone talking at the same low-energy tone... no changes, no idea when something they mention is MORE important or less so... you loose attention. The common element to both of these is lack of tone differentiation when speaking, which kills a natural way of following someone. Think about a really good story teller: they mover between low-drama tone to high-drama tone as the plot requires. 

Incidentally, I am a professional lecturer for about 30 years and a professor of social and organisational behaviour.

I have listened to him and, at the same time, reflected on my reactions, including negative ones (it's part of my regular reflexivity self-training). He does NOT speak very fast. He speaks with high level emotional excitement for the whole talk. Rather than modulate his speech, going from soft to more excited and back to less activated tone, he keeps it all in VERY HIGH EMOTIONAL tones. The consequence is that, for some people, it makes it hard to follow and they disengage after a while.

It is like the mirror image of too low activation in talking: you know, when you listen to someone talking at the same low-energy tone... no changes, no idea when something they mention is MORE important or less so... you loose attention. The common element to both of these is lack of tone differentiation when speaking, which kills a natural way of following someone. Think about a really good story teller: they mover between low-drama tone to high-drama tone as the plot requires. 

Incidentally, I am a professional lecturer for about 30 years and a professor of social and organisational behaviour.

They're laughing because everybody does it. US Standard English is not a fixed language. It constantly borrows to signal status, authority, or "coolness."

AAVE and LGBTQ+ Culture: Borrowed to gain "social capital" and appear trendy (e.g., slay, cap, tea), often resulting in the dilution of the original cultural meaning.

Luxury & Prestige Brands: Borrowed to signal "aesthetic value" and exclusivity. This includes descriptors like Bespoke, Curated, and Elevated.

Institutional & "Therapy Speak": Borrowed from HR departments and clinical psychology to make personal feelings sound objective and unassailable (e.g., bandwidth, gaslighting, circle back, unpacking).

The AI "Threat": We noted the irony of the current backlash against "AI-speak" (words like delve). While critics fear LLMs are making speech "stiff," this is simply the latest in a long-standing human habit: borrowing language to create certain impressions.

US Standard English is a blend of various dialects and speech communities. We are performing a form of linguistic LARPing by using specialized jargon to navigate a world where our social, professional, and digital identities have completely merged. Interesting perspective. I wonder if the bigger issue isn’t just distorted representations, but a shift in how language evolves once human and AI outputs continuously feed back into one another. That seems like a structural change, not just an amplification problem.

Throughout the talk, Adam Aleksic draws on etymology and contemporary social media phenomena to illustrate how algorithms shape what we see and, consequently, how we perceive reality. By highlighting how platforms prioritize the most engaging and extreme content, Aleksic argues that what we often consider rational or objective is, in fact, filtered through subjective and commercially driven systems. He also emphasizes that AI is not neutral, but rather reflects the biases embedded in its training data, encouraging viewers to adopt a more critical approach to both technology and information consumption. However, as I continued watching, I began to feel that the talk itself subtly guides the audience toward a particular way of thinking. While this may be intentional as a rhetorical strategy, it raises questions about whether the act of promoting critical thinking can itself become a form of influence.

Today’s trends seem to follow social media, including rap, electronic music, different kinds of apparel, and the Labubu example mentioned in the TED Talk. There is also a huge amount of commercial promotion behind these trends, using celebrities to create hotspots and attract people’s attention. From a psychological point of view, this makes people feel that “if I don’t have it or I don’t like it, I am out of place or out of fashion,” especially among young people. But is this really a social media or new-age issue? I don’t think so. Jazz in the 1920s, rock in the 1960s and 1970s, Pokémon cards, and brand brainwashing in the age of traditional advertising all became popular without the internet. These trends existed long before social media.

When talking about AI, the author mentions that AI does not change our thoughts directly, but rather affects our perceptions in a subtle way. However, I have a different opinion. Common stereotypes—such as North Koreans being feudalistic, Iranians being conservative, or women being bad drivers—did not emerge with AI or even with the internet. These ideas are related to psychology and the structure of the human brain. The cognitive simplification mechanism described by the author is an intrinsic characteristic of the human brain, not something created by the AI era. In psychology, the human brain prioritizes attention, working memory capacity, and cognitive energy, so people naturally rely on stereotypes and summary judgments. This is a survival mechanism, not a result of brainwashing.

In the talk, it is mentioned that Iranians are conservative. This judgment does not come out of thin air, but is based on political systems, religion, and historical context. Although there are open-minded individuals, Iranian society is relatively conservative compared to other countries. Therefore, over-attributing this pre-existing, historically formed perception to AI risks confusing cause and effect. AI itself is trained on existing knowledge, including information from the internet and self-published media, a process academically known as large-scale pretraining. AI does not create new information but summarizes and reorganizes what already exists.

If, as the author suggests, all the information we see is what others want us to see, then where can we obtain knowledge from? Even though the internet, self-published media, and AI are biased, manipulative, and commercially motivated, they remain essential tools through which we understand the world.

All in all, Adam Aleksic keenly captures the amplifying effect of algorithms on expression from both a linguistic and a content-creator perspective. However, while emphasizing the risks of technology, his argument weakens the role of human cognitive structures, commercial marketing traditions, and historical continuity, thus over-technologizing a long-standing social phenomenon. Thirty years ago, parents thought radio would ruin children; twenty years ago, it was television; ten years ago, it was smartphones and self-publishing. The author’s thinking reflects a classic form of technological anxiety. While these technologies do have an impact, overall their long-term effects tend to outweigh their disadvantages.
